Riphath
RY-fath
n. (proper name; second son of Gomer, son of Japheth)
Hebrew Riphath, of uncertain meaning. The margin of 1 Chronicles 1:6 notes or, Diphath as it is in some copies, a difference of one Hebrew letter.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Riphath is named twice, both times in a list: “And the sons of Gomer; Ashkenaz, and Riphath, and Togarmah” (Genesis 10:3), repeated at 1 Chronicles 1:6. He is a grandson of Japheth and the brother of Ashkenaz and Togarmah, which places his descendants among the northern peoples the prophets locate beyond Israel's horizon. The Authorized Version's margin at 1 Chronicles 1:6 is honest about the textual situation: some copies read Diphath, the Hebrew resh and daleth differing by a stroke. The dictionary records that without alarm; the Masoretic tradition preserves both readings and nothing doctrinal turns on either. What matters is the chapter he stands in. Genesis 10 is the genealogy of the whole human race from one man and his three sons, and it is the Bible's answer to every theory that makes the nations separately originated. “And hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth” (Acts 17:26). Riphath is a name and nothing more to us; he is a father of nations in the only account of human origins God has given.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): Riphath is a proper name and has no entry in Webster's dictionary of the English language.

expand to see more

Riphath is a Hebrew proper name; Webster's 1828 dictionary treats common English words and does not define it.

The name appears in the Table of Nations, Genesis 10:3 and 1 Chronicles 1:6.

He is the second named son of Gomer, the firstborn of Japheth.

His brothers are Ashkenaz and Togarmah, both named again in Ezekiel's oracles.

The margin of 1 Chronicles 1:6 records the variant Diphath.

Key Scripture

Gen 10:3 — "And the sons of Gomer; Ashkenaz, and Riphath, and Togarmah."

1Ch 1:6 — "And the sons of Gomer; Ashchenaz, and Riphath, and Togarmah."

Act 17:26 — "And hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth, and hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation;"

Modern Corruption

The Table of Nations is widely treated as late ethnographic myth; Scripture gives it as the genealogy of the one human race.

expand to see more

Genesis 10 is routinely handled as a post-exilic schematisation of the known world rather than as Mosaic record. The dictionary holds Mosaic authorship and the historicity of Noah and his three sons. The chapter is not a map of what Israel happened to know; it is the account of how the nations came to be, and the apostle preaches it at Athens as fact.

The principle to recover is the unity of the race. One blood, one Adam, one flood, one family of Noah — which is why Scripture knows nothing of autonomous racial categories and why every man is a neighbour and a kinsman. Riphath's descendants and Israel's share a great-grandfather.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Riphath, meaning uncertain; second son of Gomer in the Table of Nations, with the marginal variant Diphath.

expand to see more

Hebrew Riphath; the meaning is not recoverable with certainty.

1 Chronicles 1:6 margin: or, Diphath as it is in some copies.

The Hebrew letters resh and daleth differ by a single stroke.

Gomer, his father, is the firstborn of Japheth.

Ashkenaz and Togarmah, his brothers, reappear in Ezekiel 27 and 38.
